subject: chemistry
title: Partial pressures and Kp
key_idea: For gaseous equilibria, Kp is written using partial pressures instead of concentrations. A partial pressure is the mole fraction of a gas multiplied by the total pressure. Kp has units that depend on the equation, and solids are left out.

blocks.text: In a mixture of gases, each gas contributes part of the total pressure. That part is its partial pressure.

items.meaning: The moles of one gas divided by the total moles of gas in the mixture.
The pressure a gas would exert if it alone occupied the container: its mole fraction × the total pressure.

blocks.label: Mole fraction
blocks.formula: mole fraction of X = moles of X ÷ total moles of gas

blocks.label: Partial pressure
blocks.formula: p(X) = mole fraction of X × total pressure
where: p(X) = partial pressure of X, in Pa, kPa or atm
total pressure in the same unit

items: The mole fractions of all the gases add up to 1.
The partial pressures add up to the total pressure.

diagram.alt: Practise finding a partial pressure from moles of gas and total pressure.
diagram.question: A mixture contains **{n} mol** of gas X out of **{t} mol** of gas in total, at a total pressure of **{P} kPa**. Calculate the partial pressure of X.

items: Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure.
Mole fractions add to 1 and partial pressures add to the total pressure.

blocks.text: Kp is the equilibrium constant calculated from partial pressures for a gas-phase system at constant temperature.

blocks.label: Kp for aA(g) + bB(g) ⇌ cC(g) + dD(g)
where: p(X) = equilibrium partial pressure of X
a, b, c, d = coefficients in the balanced equation

items: The layout is the same as Kc: products over reactants, each to the power of its coefficient.
In a heterogeneous equilibrium, only gases appear. Solids and liquids are left out.
Example: CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) has Kp = p(CO₂).
Units come from cancelling, for example atm⁻¹ or Pa². Some Kp values have no units.

items.text: At equilibrium, a 3.0 atm mixture of N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ contains 0.40 mol N₂O₄ and 0.20 mol NO₂.

items: Kp uses partial pressures of gases only.
Find mole fractions, then partial pressures, then substitute.
Work out the units by cancelling.
Temperature changes the value of Kp.
Total pressure changes the position of equilibrium, but not the value of Kp.
A catalyst makes equilibrium arrive sooner, but does not change Kp.
A pressure rise moves the position to the side with fewer moles of gas, until the ratio equals Kp again.
Only temperature changes Kp.
Pressure can shift the position without altering Kp.

checks.q: A gas mixture contains 2.0 mol N₂ and 6.0 mol H₂ at a total pressure of 400 kPa. Calculate the partial pressure of H₂.
checks.a: Mole fraction of H₂ = 6.0 ÷ 8.0 = 0.75. p(H₂) = 0.75 × 400 = 300 kPa.

checks.q: Write the expression for Kp for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g).
Write the expression for Kp for C(s) + CO₂(g) ⇌ 2CO(g) and give its units if pressures are in atm.
checks.a: Kp = p(CO)² ÷ p(CO₂), with the solid left out. Units: atm.

items: Solids and liquids have constant concentrations, so they are left out of heterogeneous Kc and Kp expressions.
Calculations of Kc and Kp, or related quantities, include working out the units.
You will not be asked to solve a quadratic equation.
Give partial pressures in atm, so Kp units are written in atm.
Calculate Kc and Kp from experimental data for both homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, with units where appropriate.
Predict the qualitative effect of temperature and pressure on the position of equilibrium.
Predict the qualitative effect of temperature on the value of Kp: it rises for an endothermic reaction and falls for an exothermic reaction as temperature increases.
A catalyst can change the rate of reaching equilibrium, but not the value of the equilibrium constant.
You do not need the relationship between Kp and Kc.
Kc and Kp calculations will not need quadratic equations.
